extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly; students and scholars of sociology and social theory; general educated public interested in comparative social structures
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative-historical exposition identifying the structural traits and social consequences of the 'militant' type of society (how habitual militancy shapes institutions, roles, property, and values). Uses ethnographic and historical examples (Dahomey, Incas, Egypt, Sparta, Rome, Russia, modern Germany, Britain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fighting body coextensive with adult male population
rubrics_metrics.description: The fighting body is habitually coextensive with the adult male population — i.e., most adult males are part of the combatant force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as a familiar fact for small primitive groups; cited as a basic structural feature indicating militant organization (no specific scoring guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Women in servile position and role as permanent commissariat
rubrics_metrics.description: Women occupy a servile position, do the unskilled labor, bear burdens, and often carry supplies during war — serving as the permanent commissariat for the fighting class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bhils and Khonds (Asia), New Caledonians and Sandwich-Islanders (Polynesia), Comanches, Mundrucus, Patagonians (America). Used to indicate gendered labor division in militant societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of captives/enslaved people to support combatant class
rubrics_metrics.description: Where enslaving of captives has arisen, captives serve to support and aid the combatant class — acting in peace as producers and in war attending the army or carrying provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New-Zealanders, Malagasy. Cited as another means by which non-combatant labor supports the militant organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public claims override private claims; individual subordinated to group needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Private claims are overridden by public claims: the life, freedom, and goods of each person are held subject to the needs of the group; private property is limited or suspended during war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Brazilian Indians (personal property scarcely recognized during war), accounts of hyperborean tribes. Presented as a defining legal/social relationship in militant types.

rubrics_metrics.name: War initiates political subordination and creates/channels chiefship
rubrics_metrics.description: In societies without prior political subordination, war initiates it: a chief is tacitly or overtly acknowledged during conflict and gains permanent power if war continues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as a causal mechanism for the genesis of political headship from military leadership; general theoretical claim illustrated by multiple cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme ruler with divine or supernatural character and absolute authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A ruler who is absolute and regarded as supernatural or divinely descended, combining political, religious, and judicial authority and absorbing all powers and rights into the person of the ruler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Dahomey (king regarded as 'the spirit'), the Inca (divinely descended ruler), ancient Egypt. Guidance: used to identify highly centralized militant states where the ruler's person embodies state authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensive regimentation of names, ranks, dress, and sumptuary laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed regimentation where names, ranks, clothing, weapons, and honors are strictly controlled and often assigned by the ruler; numerous ranks/dignities with sumptuary laws restricting personal alteration without permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Dahomey (names change with rank; prohibitions under penalty), Inca prescriptions of clothing and badges, Egypt's elaborate class structures. Indicates tight social control and hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minutely controlled domestic life under public inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic life is regulated and subject to public/judicial inspection: people must keep houses, clothes, furniture in order; judges inspect homes; failure to conform is punished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Inca requirement to 'dine and sup with open doors' so judges may enter; Egyptian regime where every man had to account how he earned his livelihood under threat of death. Shows extension of state oversight into private life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory military service and regimented labor allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Military service is obligatory for capable individuals; those who serve form reserves and are then placed under state superintendence; labor and land allocation are organized by the state in support of the army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Incas — obligatory military service, organized army with heads of tens, fifties, hundreds, etc.; also Roman and modern examples of levies and reserves. Demonstrates institutional link between military needs and labor organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimization or absence of private property and market exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: Private property is limited; there is little or no money economy; trade is reduced to barter, and personal property is held by favor of the sovereign rather than as individual right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Inca 'they had no money... they neither sold clothes nor houses'; tribal examples where property 'ceased to be private' at war. Used as a hallmark of militant economies subordinating private exchange to state needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized hierarchical social classes aligned with military organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Society is divided into pronounced classes (priests, soldiers, townsmen/traders, common people, slaves) often with many suborders; occupational inheritance and caste-like specialization support the militant apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Egypt (four great divisions with many orders), Rome (superposed aristocracies), Sparta (Spartans, Helots, Perioiki). Indicates social stratification mirroring military roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative expansion, bureaucratization, and heavy demands on producers
rubrics_metrics.description: Growth in number and definiteness of social divisions and an extended administrative organization with numerous officials and offices that increase drafts on producers and central control over resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Augustus creating many offices and municipal officers; Roman administrative extension in provinces reducing producers to commissariat; modern German/state examples of expanded bureaucracy and taxation. Shows economic burden of sustaining a militant state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military personnel acquiring civil functions; civil roles militarized
rubrics_metrics.description: The structural character of an army spreads so that military officers take civil posts and civil functionaries assume military characteristics or authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Under Augustus and later Roman empire, military prefects acquired civil power; in Germany officers rewarded with civil appointments, and university teachers serving as officers. Indicates blurring of civil-military boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: State assumption of industrial and infrastructural functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The state takes over industrial activities and infrastructure (railways, postal banking, distribution of essential goods), extending its role into economic and commercial spheres for military or regulatory purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Prussia/Germany transferring railways to state hands (partly for military aims); postal service receiving money on bills, procuring books for shopkeepers; protectionist tariffs, usury laws. Demonstrates economic centralization tied to militancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression of dissent, censorship, and restriction of civil liberties
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures to close societies, suppress periodicals, forbid books, impose partial states of siege, penalize clergy for political opposition — i.e., active suppression of political dissent and free expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: late-19th-century German laws closing socialist societies and periodicals, forbidding books; measures to curtail local interference with police. Marks the coercive political dimension of militant regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of military discipline to police and civic institutions; centralization reducing popular checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Police and civic agencies increasingly adopt military discipline, uniforms, arms, and attitudes; executive authority overrides other agencies, and popular checks on power are weakened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: British police adopting helmet-shaped hats and revolvers and tracking 'uncertain' civilians; steps toward centralizing local police control in home office; Parliament voting multi-year military appropriations in Germany that erode popular checks. Shows diffusion of military norms into civilian governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural valorization of physical vigor and bravery
rubrics_metrics.description: Societies successful in war reward bodily vigor and courage; cultural ideals equate virtue with bravery, valorizing physical prowess over other moral qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Egyptian and Assyrian records praising prowess; Greek and Roman identification of virtue with daring and strength; medieval knightly code. Used as a characteristic value system underpinning the militant type.
